query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack, high-entropy alloys develop an ultra‐nanostructured surface layer (via dynamic grain refinement and local amorphization) that serves as a dense, self‐healing passive barrier. This layer both absorbs mechanical deformation and limits aggressive ion permeation, thereby governing resistance to combined wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a relatively coarse-grained, homogeneous solid solution microstructure before deformation (e.g. CoCrFeMnNi or a similar composition designed for harsh environments).
generation.intervention: Expose samples to simultaneous abrasive/contact wear under a corrosive environment (e.g. 3.5 wt% NaCl) so that mechanical sliding/impact induces local microstructural refinement.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at controlled loads and sliding speeds in an electrolyte environment; comparison against tests run under inert (dry or inert gas) conditions and in static immersion (no wear) so that synergies between wear and corrosion can be isolated.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous top layer (passive film) generated during the wear process.
generation.mechanism: Wear-induced dynamic grain refinement and partial amorphization result in a finely structured, chemically homogenized surface. This layer acts as a self‐renewing barrier that reduces mechanical material removal and impedes electrolyte penetration, stabilizing the passive film and reducing localized corrosion (including pitting).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy with a coarser microstructure, the alloy undergoing the combined degradation will develop a more refined, continuous passive layer that correlates with lower wear rates, decreased friction coefficients, and enhanced corrosion resistance (lower corrosion current density and improved impedance) under simultaneous wear-corrosion testing.
generation.baseline: Identical alloy subjected either to pure wear testing in inert environment or to static immersion corrosion tests, where the beneficial dynamic formation of the nanostructured passive layer is absent or less pronounced.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold under moderate mechanical stresses and corrosive environments where the dynamic layer can form and persist; it may fail if the applied load or corrosive aggressiveness exceeds the material’s capacity for continuous passive film regeneration, or if the alloy's composition does not favor rapid grain refinement.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed kinetics of passive layer formation and its long-term stability under cyclic loadings remain to be quantified; the interplay between alloy composition, processing history, and environmental parameters may affect the magnitude of the wear-corrosion synergy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical bulk compositions. Subject one set to simultaneous wear and corrosion (e.g. sliding tests in 3.5% NaCl) and conduct detailed surface analysis (using TEM, STEM, and XRD) immediately after testing to verify the formation of an ultra-nanostructured, passive surface layer. In parallel, test a control group under only wear (in inert medium) and only corrosion (static immersion) and compare the surface film structures and degradation rates.
measurements: Surface microstructure (grain size, amorphous content) via TEM/STEM
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization to assess passive film quality
Wear rate and friction coefficient measurements
Surface chemical composition analysis (EDS/ XPS) of the passive film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simultaneous wear-corrosion test does not result in a significantly finer, continuous passive surface layer compared to the baseline conditions, or if the mechanical/corrosion performance is not improved (or is worse) than that of the comparators, then the hypothesis that dynamic formation of an ultra-nanostructured passive layer governs the simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance will be falsified.

Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film

Abstract: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding

Abstract: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
